utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First, the Chamber apologises for the late start. An incredible small series of small unfortunate events kept my attention away from this courtroom where it usually is solidly focused on. We move into closed session, and could the witness be escorted into the courtroom once we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rule 67 after the first break. I leave it to that at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DST-051 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DST-051. We apologise for our late start. Some -- there was some reasons why we couldn't start any earlier. I also apologise for being very impolite in going on with discussions with the parties when you entered the courtroom. Again, apologies for that. We'll continue in a second, but I'd first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you would speak the truth -- oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the interpretation. I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you miss everything I said before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologised for the late start, I will not repeat the reasons. I also apologised for being impolite and not -- in continuing in my discussion with the parties when you entered the courtroom instead of stopping and say welcome to you. And then I reminded you, as I do now again, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Then, Mr. Groome will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I ask that we return to the screen 65 ter 6205. That's the document that we were working with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, DST-051.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Make sure I have -- did you have an opportunity to read that article over the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we go to e-court page 7. While that's being called up, are you familiar with the report that is -- is included in this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that report from reviewing the documents that I received yesterday to analyse, and if you allow, I will ask the Trial Chamber to say a few sentences about these two documents, because the Chamber deserves to know the real truth. I would like to enable you thereby to avoid wasting time on things that are useless for this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you may address the Court to make your observations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I perused the two documents very carefully. There is this article from 2004 and a document entitled "Report to the State Security Centre in Belgrade," dated 15 March 2001. I would like to direct your attention to three paragraphs in the article published in "Vreme." Page 2, Article -- or paragraph 3, and I can point out to you that this is a fake document full of false information and maliciously drafted in 2001. On page 2 of the report published in "Vreme," the third paragraph givens with "Zoran Mijatovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what page number you're looking at, and this way we can all see it. We can't see what you have there, but you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So we can call that up now on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from "Vreme."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- this is the document you want to comment on, the one you see on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. The Prosecution has a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- summary of the translation now. It's not an actual summary. I meant to say that a full translation is being done, so it's not possible to look at the actual text that he's referring to. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but is the -- original is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the document on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the right. Okay. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is not the page I mean, the one I see on the screen. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has referred repetitiously to the "Vreme" article. Is this the "Vreme" article or is it not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Vreme."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, but we're on e-court page 7. I think if we go to e-court page 2 you'll be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 1. This is page. In paragraph 3 of this text, Zoran Mijatovic, the journalist who writes for "Vreme," states that immediately after taking over duty after the elections held in Serbia 2001, he tasked to his co-workers to investigate into the cases that Djindjic wanted to be clarified. He tasked an operative whose initials are ZS. I know who that is, but out of respect for this Court and the accused, I don't want to mention his name. It shouldn't be recorded in the transcript. Zoran Mijatovic says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Why should it not be recorded, respect for the accused, respect for the Court, if you know the name? The reasons you gave are not such -- that if you want to respect the Court, you should leave the decision to the Court whether or not the name should be mentioned or not. So we invite you to give the name if you know who this person is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you demand me to do it, I can state the name. The name is Zoran Stijovic. It was his task to conduct an internal investigation within the State Security Service of Serbia with regard to the circumstances I'm discussing now. What is interesting here is that Mr. Zoran Mijatovic, who was then the deputy head of the State Security Service, refers to the Serbian Prime Minister, Zoran Djindjic, ordering an investigation. Knowing the late Mr. Djindjic - I knew him personally - and I know he was a democrat, I cannot believe or moreover I'm sure that the prime minister of Serbia at that time could have ordered what ZS did during the internal investigation in the service. Mr. Mijatovic, in the third paragraph, says that they interviewed over 180 people. He says: "Because of the destruction of documents and other serious crimes such as weapons trafficking, unauthorised surveillance, and others, we arrested 180 people." Your Honours, in a small State Security Service such as that of Serbia, subject 180 people to operative treatment meant that from the lowest level to the top, namely to the chief of the operative section or group, everybody would have had to be involved in that action. Mr. ZS, whose name I've mentioned, had many people on his list who were to be arrested. In one interview Mr. Zoran Mijatovic, the then deputy, informed me, I was head of the State Security Centre in Nis, that he had an order to arrest us, but he failed to mention that it was an order of the prime minister Zoran Djindjic because I wouldn't have believed him. That internal investigation took a long time. A hundred and eighty members of the service were subjected to operative and technical activities and measures. Can you imagine that any court or let alone the president of the Supreme Court of Serbia would have ordered -- would have signed an order to place 180 members of the service under surveillance? I can't imagine that. Once they were replaced, a commission found out that there was a grave misuse in the -- or abuse of power in this investigation against 180 people. One of my colleagues was interrogated, and to say that they used the methods of the Inquisition would be an understatement. If they could collect false documents about our alleged crimes, they would get some advantages. I was also on that list, among the first dozen or so, and there were dozens of people on that list. Some people were interrogated very harshly. Psychological pressure was exerted on them, and unfortunately, some of them are no longer alive due to that. And the following stayed after this internal investigation. There was a -- there were pre-criminal proceedings, and during these proceedings, people were also interrogated. You see that it says here that criminal reports were filed. However, an honest and fair prosecutor at the District Court in Belgrade refused to launch an investigation against these 180 people. There are documents about that. And I'm surprised why the state of Serbia does not give you genuine documents but instead gives you fake documents that compromise me and other people before this Court. This is what I have to say. And the last sentence, by this forging of things, the -- these people from the service did not protect the constitutional order, and nor did they protect personalities, the consequence of which was that the democratically elected president was shot dead in front of the government building because they weren't doing their job. They were dealing with false accusations against their colleagues. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir -- DST-051, I want to try to clarify some of the things now you've said. You've spoken for quite some time. I just want to ask you if you can answer some questions simply "yes" or "no" just to confirm that we have understand -- or I have understood correctly. The article which is 65 ter 6205, you dispute much of its contents; is that correct? A simple yes or no if you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't dispute the article that you've read, that you've just talked about. Do you agree with it's contents, or do you disagree with of its contents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree with the contents of the article. It was written based on false documents. The article as such is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you do seem to confirm that there was an internal investigation by the State Security Service; is that correct? That there was some internal investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You also seem to confirm that you were one of the people who was investigated in this internal investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the investigation -- was the allegation being investigated related to destruction of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, when the results of the investigation were referred to a criminal prosecutor, a public prosecutor, the case was not pursued in a criminal court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you made a statement that the -- you were surprised that the Serbian government had given the court fake documents. Are you referring to the documents that are cited by the author of this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean this report, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I've showed -- yesterday I showed you a number of documents provided by your government. You did -- you're not saying that those documents were forgeries, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that only this document is fake, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we clarified that. Could we go back now to e-court page 7. I wanted to focus on one item. It's number 15 on a list of documents that were alleged to have been destroyed. Could I ask you to simply read item 15. Can you simply read that aloud so that we can have it translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Destroy documents related to collaborators, associates for special purposes, insofar as the centres had these."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you with your experience help us understand. What would collaborators and associates for special purposes -- what type of person would that refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit to the Trial Chamber and to you that for the first time in my practice have I now seen this term, associate for special purposes. I'm not familiar with this term, but that doesn't mean that there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that 65 ter 6205 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections, or not yet of any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the -- the -- it's a query as much as an objection as to the precise relevance. If it's relevant to the witness's credibility, that's one thing. If it's relevant to the charges directly, that's another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not seeking to tender it at this moment. This document will be used with future witnesses, and at that stage if the Prosecution feels there's a proper basis, it will move to admit the document. It simply seeks to mark it for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But that's just avoiding the issue as to what is the preliminary relevance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Evidence has to be relevant. I do understand that the establishment of the relevance of this document would not be limited to one witness but would be presented through more witnesses and then the decision on the relevance of this document as an exhibit would be -- would then be sought by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would like to, and I think I might have to, but then again I might not have to, re-examine on the subject depending upon its alleged relevance with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only question I had intended to ask this witness was to read 15 and whether he could interpret that for us. He says that he is unable to assist us. All of the other questions I asked related to this document was just to clarify what the witness wanted to volunteer about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question. The question still remains why did we go through that process. If the Prosecution have not considered what its relevance is, then it ought not to be admitted even as an MFI document, and we ought not to have gone through that process. If they have considered what its relevance is, even minimal relevance, we ought to be told in [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, first of all, I don't think it would be the best thing to do, to discuss the relevance in the presence of the witness. Therefore, Mr. Groome, if you would like to respond to that, I would give you an opportunity the last minute before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can save us all some trouble. We can just simply recall it at a later stage by the 65 ter number. The record is clear what document we've used. It's not essential that it be given an identification number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, of course the advantage of having it marked for identification is that any discussion about what document questions were asked about is eliminated. That's the only purpose at this moment. And I do understand for marking it for identification, that a question was put in relation to this very document. Whether we do it by 65 ter number or whether we do it by an MFI number might not be that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will -- if that's the situation, I'll be re-examining blind, because I really don't know what the point of this document is. It relates to a period long after the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You're free to make up your mind as to what questions you would like to put to the witness in re-examination. That's not for the Chamber to decide that. The situation is clear at this moment. The document will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2979, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any need to have it under seal or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, DST-051 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the Defence needs a little while to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DST-051, during the course of this trial there has been some evidence about the Serbian Volunteer Guard, also known as Arkan's men, and the vehicles that they had, a vehicle with the emblem of the organisation on the side. My question to you is: Have you ever seen that vehicle in your work, vehicles with the Serbian Volunteer Guard insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now turn your attention to the attack on Bosanski Samac. The Chamber has heard evidence that this commenced on the 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that P1425 be brought to our screens, and could we please focus on the top half of the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DST-051, we've seen Slobodan Miljkovic's name on the list. Do you have any knowledge about what his relationship was with the State Security Service? I'll read the passage of this letter I wish you to comment on, but do you know what the relationship was between Lugar and the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Defence asked me about Veljkovic [as interpreted], I said that to my knowledge concerning Slobodan Veljkovic [as interpreted], was never in any organised relationship with the SDB. He was operationally treated in the sense of his opposition to extremist activity. I don't know who wrote this document that was supposedly sent to the Kragujevac branch of the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- whether Lugar is living or dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've explained in my testimony that Lugar, in 1998, was killed by members of the SDB -- or, actually, by Mr. Lukovic. I think it was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I said so when I was examined by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise if I missed that, but -- so you're saying that in 1998, Lugar, Slobodan Miljkovic, was killed by members of the State Security Service. Can you tell us the circumstances under which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already have, but I'd be happy to repeat. Slobodan Miljkovic, for a number of years exhibited significant hatred towards the State Security Centre and its members in Kragujevac. His background is quite different, and that is why he hated the members of our service. Our colleague, Mr. Lukovic, committed that murder in a restaurant in Kragujevac. He was the son of an anti-fascist hero who fought in World War II, and at the same time, on the other side, there were relatives of Slobodan Veljkovic [as interpreted], Lugar. They were part of the Chetnik Movement, and these were two ideologically opposed sides in that war. Since Lukovic was the son of a World War II hero, he was exposed to bursts of anger and hatred by Lugar. He would cut his tyres and do such things. When the murder took place --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure we need all of the detail about it, but it seems that you're now saying Lukovic murdered Lugar? Is that your understanding of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After his murder, his lawyer provided number of documents to the Office of the Prosecutor and a copy of the letter you now see on the screen before us as P1425. I want to read you a short passage of that letter which is in evidence: "In 1992, I went to Lezimir Pajzos with a unit for special physical training. After having completed the training, as a platoon commander I was transferred by helicopter to Bosnia (Batkusa near Samac). Then I had the task to attack the town of Bosanski Samac and occupy one of the most important points (the State Security Service). The operation to seize the town was completed in a record time of 37 minutes." Having heard Lugar's account that was given to the State Security Service in this letter, do you -- would you acknowledge that he -- that the State Security Service played a direct role in the attack on Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that the SDB centre in Kragujevac played any role in the attack on Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The document is dated the 11th of March, 1996. In 1995, the BBC published a documentary in which Vojislav Seselj in a videotaped interview stated what -- was asked about what happened in Zvornik, and he said: "This was devised by key people from the SDB, amongst whom was Franko Simatovic, Frenki, and he was one of the main executors. Our volunteers gathered and their central meeting point was in Loznica from where they headed towards Zvornik. Duk [phoen] Cvijetinovic was in charge and he directly received orders from the commander of the special units." This is Exhibit P18 in this case. You or senior law enforcement officer. Is it ever appropriate for a person publicly named as a participant in an event to be involved in the investigation into that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the extent I understood the Prosecutor, he quoted from an interview given by Vojislav Seselj to the BBC in 1995 or 1996. I fail to understand that I'm being asked before this Court to comment on Seselj's interviews given to international news agencies and the like. If you think that these interviews are serious, then I must say that I haven't read the interview, and I'm not willing to comment on it. Seselj has said so many things in 10 or 15 years that there's nobody who can keep track of all of that and to tell right from wrong, and I'm really not willing to listen to Seselj's speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my question is actually something far simpler. Is it ever appropriate for a person who has been publicly identified as a participant in an event to be involved into the investigation of that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically, no, but I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the real goal behind Operation Tompson was not to bring war criminals to justice but to deal with the problem that these very dangerous people, armed with weapons, the danger that they presented to the citizens of Serbia when they returned home from committing their crimes in places like Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main goal of Operative Action Thomson is precisely stated in the decision on the establishment and the implementation of the operative action. I'm certain that all my colleagues in Serbia, and they did investigate all extremism there, that during the period from 1991 onward, they were able to come by judicial documents about war crimes -- or, rather, if they had been able to do that, they would have seen to it that these persons stand trial. They were dealing with extremism, and one form of -- one form of extremism is committing war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Jordash, towards the end of his examination of you yesterday asked a similar question, and I'm going to read it to you, and nowhere in the answer did you say it was about bringing war criminals to justice. This is at T-11712: "During the period from the launch of the operative action in mid-1991 and through mid-1995, I believe when all organisational units of the State Security Service, 18 of them, gave their respective contributions for the analysis of the results of the Operative Action Tompson, it becomes clear that the State Security Service of Serbia, together with the public security service, implemented a number of measures daily, from surveillance of the persons involved in the Tompson operation, the confiscation of large quantities of weapons, filing criminal reports for illegal possession of weapons, and so on, all the way through to something that can't be seen in these documents; namely, preventative actions in order to prevent the spill-over of war activities into Serbia." Isn't the truth that you were concerned that these people might start killing Muslim civilians, Muslim Serbian civilians, living in places like Sandzak? Isn't that the real reason, the real goal behind Operation Tompson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you began quoting my -- something I said yesterday, something was wrongly translated, namely that we contributed to the analysis, right at the beginning, that the SDB members contributed to the analysis of the Tompson action. I don't have the text, but it should be contributed to the implementation. The analysis was made in 1996, because it turns out that SDB members from mid-1991 through mid-1996 were analysing something that they were in the course of carrying out. So it shouldn't be analysis, but it should be contributed to the implementation or the carrying out of the tasks from the Tompson operative action.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you blamed our interpreters and transcribers for this mistake. Is there any chance that you expressed yourself not accurately? We'll check it on the basis of the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you start blaming others for mistakes, would you also have a look at the possibility that you made a mistake. We will verify it on the basis of the audio. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, out of the combined work of the 18 operational units of the State Security Service, of all the people surveilled and investigated, apart from the Vuckovic brothers, those two brothers, how many individuals were referred for prosecution to the courts of Serbia for war crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the question. However, there is a problem concerning the 18 centres of the State Security Service and the results of Operative Action Tompson. It is difficult for me to understand, and I believe I said so to the Defence as well, that the SDB received 18 reports from the centres about the implementation of the Tompson action. The analysis of the Fifth Analytical Department of the SDB was to take all 18 reports, collate them, and carry out an analysis of the results of the Operative Action Tompson. That analysis, I presume, was put on some 30 or so pages. You asked me whether I could read that analytical document. If I had, I would have been able to provide precise answers. It is unclear to me why neither you nor the Defence received that analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spend a lot of words, but apparently as far as I see - but I could be wrong, Mr. Groome - you missed the core of the question. The question by Mr. Groome was: In how many cases, apart from the two Vuckovic brothers, how many cases could you tell us -- how'd all these activities, in how many cases they resulted before a court? Who sent what? I think Mr. Groome is mainly interested to see the activities described, whether 18 or 17 or 19, whether directly reporting, indirectly reporting, this resulted in how many cases that were brought before courts in Serbia? That's the question, Mr. Groome, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer that question. If you know, tell us. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a number of reports, although I cannot recall how many off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, the question was: How many cases were brought before the court, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've referred to a document, this analytical summary or some analytical report. Is it your evidence that there is a document generated by the State Security Service which referred identified individuals for prosecution before the courts of Serbia for war crimes committed outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not assert that such a document exists. What I assert is that there is an analysis of the results of Operative Action Tompson. It is a document that the leadership of the service was familiar with, including Mr. Jovica Stanisic as the chief of the service. Here you have 18 reports which only form part of the overall reports from the centres. It is not a complete set of information. Somewhere in the service there must be this analytical document which was created in the latter part of 1996, and it seems you did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us as best you're able, and with as much precision as you're able, the name of the document? What should we request from your government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you put one of the reports back on the screen that mentioned the analysis, I might be able to say that the theme or the topic for that year was analysis of the results and forthcoming tasks of Operative Action Tompson. That was the topic requested by the leadership of the service. The Fifth Analytical Administration was collecting information up until mid-1996, and in the second part of 1996, all those 18 reports containing hundreds of pages were put together in a single document, which is called: "Analysis of the Implementation and Results of Operative Action Thomson and Further Tasks." I was looking at that document, and Mr. Stanisic was familiar with it because he was the head of that team on behalf of the State Security Service regarding Operative Action Tompson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During -- or towards the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination of DST-051. The Prosecution does ask that a Defence exhibit, 1D01121, be marked for identification. It is an internal report of the State Security Service, dated the 1st of April, 1995, providing a historical account of the activities of extremists and paramilitaries in Bosnia. This report appears to be constructed from analysis of source documents from the period 1991 to 1993. We were given notice it would be used with this witness, but ultimately it was not. I ask for it to be marked for identification at this stage. The Prosecution will undertake an investigation into its authenticity and report to the Chamber about any further applications we might make regarding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against this document to be MFI'd? Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit P2981, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, no need to have the document under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a Defence document. I'll be guided by Mr. Jordash on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be under seal then. It's marked for identification as P2981 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I will take the opportunity to indicate on the record that previously marked document P2980 is also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record as well. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, new questions arose from cross-examination by Mr. Groome that I would like to address in redirect, and I presume we will keep the order as usual, and I will be guided by your instruction on when and how best to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By using the word "redirect," you suggest that this is your witness, and I did understand that despite Rule 90(H) that you had cross-examined the witness. But let's be very practical. If you would save your questions until after Mr. Jordash has used, if he wishes to do so, his right to re-examine the witness. That's redirect, I would say. And then you could even put questions to the witness in response to what Mr. Jordash asked in redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that Mr. Bakrac put his questions before I redirect since the purpose of my redirect will be to clarify issues which remain unclear or perhaps need further elaboration, in our view, and I'd like to do it knowing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- what the whole series of questions and answers have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, do you have any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to go back to two or three documents shown by Mr. Groome. Basically I'll have three or four topics, but together with the bringing up of documents, I might require between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, since all parties seem to agree on it, the Chamber does not oppose, you may put these additional questions. Please keep in mind that the time you spend on these questions is considered time which you would ordinary use after Mr. Jordash would have re-examined the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will focus only on what I believe was of interest with relation to my client during cross-examination. Could we look at D246, which is the last document shown by

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please look at 2D858.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the translation is still pending. However, it is a brief document. It is actually a criminal report referred to by Mr. Groome against the Vuckovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please have a look at it, Witness. On the left-hand side it says "The Republic of Serbia, District Public Prosecutor's Office, Sabac, May 6, 1994." The title -- or actually addressed to the Ministry of the Interior, Centre of the State Security Service in Valjevo. Thereby, they inform the Valjevo centre that an indictment was issued against Dusko Vuckovic for a war crime and the crime of rape, as well as a number of other crimes. In the second paragraph it says: "Your criminal report number mentioned above was dismissed as submitted against Vojin Vuckovic for the war crime against civilian population of Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the FRY, because there is no reason to suspect that the accused Vojin Vuckovic committed that crime." Was the Second Administration supposed to be familiar with this communication between the SDB centre and the public prosecutor in Sabac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My second question is this: Did the centre in Valjevo have the possibility to investigate in detail the information that Vojin Vuckovic provided them with in the field in the area of Zvornik and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The centre of state security in Valjevo, as part of their regular activities and tasks had no legal authority to act in Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to investigate war crimes. They could, however, collect information and gain knowledge about war crimes in their own territory in -- from such persons who appeared in their territory during the relevant time as people who returned from the RS or came there as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All the information Mr. Groome read out to you, was it forwarded to the district public prosecutor, and was it under our law -- was it up to the prosecutor to decide whether he would initiate any further criminal procedure under the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the documents assembled concerning the crimes committed by the Vuckovic brothers, including his confession he gave to the authorised officials of the SDB in Belgrade, and based on prior consultations conducted in the public prosecutor's office in Belgrade, as well as based on an agreement that the criminal report be submitted to the district prosecutor in Sabac because some activities of the Vuckovic brothers also happened there, that is why the prosecutor's office in Sabac was to deal with it. All that documentation was, for all those reasons, handed over to the public prosecutor's office in Sabac. What we can see based on this, that the prosecutor decided that there were insufficient grounds to bring any charges against one of the Vuckovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that the prosecutor, based on all this, had information about the crime committed -- allegedly committed by Marko Pejic, member of the Serb Volunteer Guard, and was it the prosecution who decided whether there was sufficient grounds to initiate any proceedings against him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe he's established the foundation that this witness could know that answer. I would ask that we explore upon what does he have this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome -- Mr. Bakrac, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Mr. Groome read out the statement of one of the Vuckovic brothers who stated that Marko Pejic was a member of the SDG. As far as I know, that information was handed over to the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what the problem of Mr. Groome is that he wonders whether you have laid a sufficient foundation that the witness would have any knowledge about the reasons for the decision and even the decision whether there was sufficient grounds to initiate any proceedings against Pejic. That apparently is what is bothering Mr. Groome. Do you have any knowledge about why and on what grounds the prosecution formed an opinion about whether there was sufficient grounds to initiate any proceedings against Pejic? Have you knowledge of that? No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have two more questions about two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday we looked at a payment list which had your name on it, and you said that you thought this represented the issuance of DSAs or per diems. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the issuance of per diems to you at that time have anything to do with Mr. Stanisic? Did he have a role within that issuance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and it wasn't only at the time when Mr. Stanisic was the head of the service but also before and after that, the heads of service never dealt with the payment of per diems. It was part of standard procedure with standard forms to be filled out, and that issue was dealt at a much lower level, usually between the operative administration and the Eighth Administration. Not even the deputy head of service discussed such issues with the chiefs of administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, the Prosecution asked you about a statement by Jovica Djordjevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that man had provided a statement to the OTP, and it made within it various allegations about the taking over of the federal MUP building. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did -- did you know Jovica Djordjevic when he was an operative worker at the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He worked in the State Security Centre in Leskovac, and he worked on domestic extremism and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he continue working in the State Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His conduct was problematic. Sometime in 1995 or 1996, although I lack precise information, the head of service established a commission comprising operative inspectors from the Third Administration, which had to review the overall operative work carried out by Jovica Djordjevic in the course of that year, although again I must specify that I'm not sure as to what year it was. It turned out that the results of their inquiry were that his work was basically a disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any consequence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the commission's conclusion -- well, the consequences were that they concluded that he should be fired, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add just one sentence. His role in the taking over of the federal MUP building was in terms of duty service --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As the witness says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and it didn't include only him but most of the people who had per diems paid out to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. One more subject, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P2979 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this Article in "Vreme" and the investigation that is referred to within. Now, am I correct that the investigation took place in 2000? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigation was initiated sometime in -- well, it says here December 2000. It began following the removal of Radomir Markovic, who was the head of the state security sector, at the moment when Zoran Mijatovic as the deputy and the chief of the service took over the service. Their first task allegedly issued to them as the prime minister, whereas it is my belief that they received the task from some other institution, was to carry out an investigation with relation to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you try to just shorten your answers a little bit. I want to ask about some very specific issues. Thank you. Did the investigation relate to state -- or purport to relate to state security activity in the year 2000 or before that? When -- when was it -- what was its target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 2000, it pertained to the period between September and the end of that year, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I think it's agreed that Mr. Stanisic left the service in 1998. Had there been any changes in the State Security Service between 1998 and 2000 which you would consider to be unhelpful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood the gist of your question, I'd say this: The investigation covering the period between September and December, that is to say from the federal elections and until the end of 2000, that investigation is, under no circumstances, connected with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm focusing on is whether you observed any changes within the State Security Service from the time Mr. Stanisic left to the point of this investigation which you considered, as a professional, unhelpful for the service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The changes were for the worse. In what sense? As in 1990 and 1991, we got a new head who had previously never dealt with state security. A number of employees of the service felt the consequences of such personnel policy decisions or choices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about between 1998 and 2000, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking about that period. What I said pertains to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Jordash, he says: "As in 1990 and 1991, we got," that is in 1998. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in a nutshell, what were those personnel policy decisions? What were those personnel policy decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the question. A number of professionals from the period, from 1992 through 1998, lost their jobs with the service. There was stronger influence from some party structures on personnel policy decisions within the service. Some people lost their positions in the service. The Yugoslav left was strongly present in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From which party did those personnel come from, or parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of the party is the Yugoslav Left. It was the party of the wife of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know what her relationship was with Mr. Stanisic at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just seems like a new area. I don't believe I've raised this in cross-examination, and I don't know -- Mr. Jordash gone into an area beyond cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know the relevance of this investigation, so I'm trying to cover everything which I think might reasonably arise from it, and if the suggestion is that this wrongdoing and this investigation had something to do with Mr. Stanisic, then the question I've just asked concerning the changes in the DB and their relationship to Milosevic's wife I think is pertinent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could imagine that, for example, the questions were raised in the context of credibility and reliability of the witness, for example, and then of course it would be a different matter, but perhaps, Mr. Groome, you could assist Mr. Jordash in considering whether he should further pursue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can give an undertaking, Your Honour, that the Prosecution will never argue that Mr. Stanisic is somehow responsible for the allegations in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is that helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then proceed. You announced 30 minutes, I think we're now at approximately 40, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I thought I was just on 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we resumed at five minutes to 6.00, where we announced ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have page 7 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have the next page of the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Groome about number 15, the "destruction of documents related to collaborators for special purposes, insofar as the centres had had these." Just to be clear, are there any DB rules which entitle operatives or the DB hierarchy to destroy documents. Is this legislated or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat that in the 30 years of my service in the state security, I've never heard of that. I can't rule out, though, that some documents provide for the existence of associates for special purposes. A colleague of mine may be able to better explain, but no documents were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was whether you're aware of any rules governing the destruction of documents. That was the question. Do you know about such regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I want to speak about. Since the service was established, there has been a rule book on the keeping and maintenance of documents. Nothing could be destroyed. We had to work in accordance with the rule book which every operative worker had to honour fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the rule book says never any document ever to be destroyed. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The rules of service say -- the rule book on documents and their maintenance regulates the manner of keeping documents and which documents may be destroyed, but only in accordance with the provisions that have rule book, not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you ever requested or have you ever heard of a request from Mr. Stanisic to destroy documents outside of those rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further. Thank you, Mr. DST-051.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Jordash. Mr. Bakrac, nothing further?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After my bad experience after my previous examination, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions of the witness, but given all of the discussion about the Vukovic brothers and the jurisdictional questions, the Prosecution would tender the indictment and judgement for that case. They're 65 ter numbers 1641 and 1647. This way I think it would be informative of the Court to be able to read the legal accusatory instrument and judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against this? Then you have mentioned the 65 ter numbers. Could numbers be assigned. It was 65 ter 1641 and 1647.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And 1641 is the indictment and 1647 is the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document bearing 65 ter 1641 will become Exhibit P2982, and the second document, 65 ter 1647, will become Exhibit P2983.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Both documents are admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe they need to be under seal. I believe they're public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I made a mistake there. It's good that you correct me immediately. Judge Picard has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good evening, sir. I want to make sure that I understood your testimony properly, therefore, I have a question for you. At the time when you were working in the MUP State Security Service, you were in the Third Administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Third Administration is the one in charge of extremist -- internal, domestic extremist and terrorist movements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I'm asking this is that many questions were put to you during these hearings as to whether you might know operatives who worked for the security service for the Second Administration. To be more precise, the administration in charge of gathering intelligence generally and for intelligence for actions or activities outside the country. Now, I must say that at times - how shall I say? - you were quite specific in your answers. You said, "No, it could not be. He could not have been an operative. He could not have worked for the State Security Service," but in fact there was no way in which you could have learned about the identity of operatives working outside the country. There was no way you could know their identity, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but I have a remark. It was not possible for somebody to be a member of the state security service, including the Second Administration, and at the same time be subjected to operative processing by the state security centre in Kragujevac, and operative processing is the most demanding and most complex type of processing. That would be my reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure I understood your answer. Could you be more specific? Could you explain some more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is this: I was shown a list of persons and asked whether they were members of the State Security Service. Those persons were on list of extremists who were subjected by operative measures by the State Security Service which countered their activities. That is why I think it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But given the situation at the time, the situation, it was war on the borders of Serbia, don't you think that these individual could have had activities outside the borders? Maybe not within Serbia, but outside Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I maintain that they should not be members. Whether it was possible, well, I am not in a position to say with full certainty that it is impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony in this courtroom, Witness DST-051. I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague. I noticed by the way, Mr. Jordash, that you have not presented the document to the witness. If you are -- you may have understood between the lines that the Chamber might be interested to once receive it in evidence. That might be your interest as well. And then, of course, not to be faced with authenticity problems -- unnecessarily faced with authenticity problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But my concern was, Your Honour, that there is many pages as I'm holding in my hands, and I didn't think it fair to ask the witness to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There, of course, might be a possibility to, perhaps in co-operation with the Prosecution, apparently also interested in knowing what the document is and what it is about, to try and find an out-of-court possibility to see whether any agreement could be reached on authenticity, perhaps with the assistance of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would have no objection to the witness being given the packet of documents tonight and if he, Mr. Jordash wishes, that he would be called first thing tomorrow and deal with it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, we're not sitting tomorrow morning. So first thing in the morning would be at 1.00. But if Mr. Jordash and you would agree on -- that this witness, at least, does not challenge the authenticity, that's established, so that if need be we could ever recall him, but I don't know whether its necessary at this point. I leave it in your hands. The only thing is let's not lose opportunities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If DST-051 doesn't mind looking at the documents and also doesn't mind coming back early tomorrow afternoon, then that would be our preferred course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know what your time schedule is as far as returning home, Witness DST-051.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me to return tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know when -- when you are scheduled to return to -- to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told by the Victims and Witnesses Unit that I was to leave tomorrow and the plane was to leave from Amsterdam at around noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in the hands of the parties what action they wish to take or not. The Chamber has done enough, I think, to draw the attention to the problem. You are excused, Witness DST-051. If you receive a copy of a certain set of documents, and I don't know whether you want to give it under the present circumstances, yes or no, then I would instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony until this obligation has been lifted by the Chamber, and that is specifically in relation to the documents which you are invited to have a look at. May I take it that Mr. Jordash and Mr. Groome will take the appropriate measures how to deal with these documents which are now given to the witness? Then I await your further initiatives. I take it that an extra copy will be given sooner or later to Mr. Groome, or if he has received it already. Witness, you're invited to have a look at those documents. Mr. Bakrac, do you still want to see it, or do you want to have a look at another copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. I believe there will be no problem in Mr. Jordash providing a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a copy is now provided to you. You're invited to have a look at those documents. You're hereby instructed not to copy them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That would take by far too much time. We give it to you. You should keep it for yourself, you should not copy them, and you should not discuss the content with anyone apart from the Prosecution and Defence. Then you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, does this mean that I have to return to the courtroom tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- no. It depends on the parties whether they'll invite you to do that. They'll certainly then immediately contact the Victims and Witness Section. They would -- at this moment it is not decided that you will return to the courtroom tomorrow. If that changes, you'll be immediately informed, and the Chamber will also be informed. I would suggest that the parties are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether you -- whether you received any instructions or whether the consultation led to any other conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it didn't. I can indicate I'm going to communicate with Mr. Groome's commission through the VWS as to the witness's practical arrangements, and we'll go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I even can imagine -- yes. Let's not. You're hereby excused for the moment. It's -- chances that you'll be called tomorrow are there but are limited, if I could say so. Please follow whatever requests you will receive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I will be extremely brief on the last matter. Mr. Groome, you have requested that the Defence would immediately meet its obligations under Rule 67, that is, to provide any statement by a witness they intend to call. That request is granted. Of course, the Chamber does not know whether there are any more than the two statements you had received. Your request to receive notes taken by those who have interviewed prospective witnesses as a substitute for compliance with Rule 67, that request is provisionally not granted. Parties are invited, Prosecution first, to make any additional submissions on the matter, the Prosecution by Wednesday the 29th of June, responses by the Defence by the 4th of July close of business. The parties are invited to address both legal aspects of the problem but also factual aspects such as how many statements have been -- were taken? Have people been interviewed? Have they -- are there -- do notes at all exist? So to give not only your legal position but also where we stand as far as facts are concerned. We will give further guidance after we received these submissions from the parties. And now I can't -- yes. I already can tell the parties that of course the function of Rule 67 is to give notice to the other party of what they can expect so as to enable them to prepare for cross-examination. There are a lot of -- of details involved such as are statements taken? Is there an obligation to take a statement? Are -- have there been any interviews? Is there an obligation to conduct any interviews? Finally, the Chamber will not easily accept a situation in which the function of Rule 67, that is giving adequate notice to the other party, would totally be undermined by a chosen practice. We'll consider all that, but if -- for example, if no more than the two statements would be ever produced, if we would have to look at a request postponement of cross-examination for every witness, thus delaying the proceedings, then the Chamber would actively seek procedural remedies for such a situation. That is the practical side. At the same time, the Chamber expects, on the basis of the submissions of the parties, also to carefully consider other elements involved in this matter such as privilege, such as the right to remain silent and not be under an obligation to incriminate yourself, but we'll finally give this total guidance after we've received your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I simply say that we can file our submissions tomorrow, and I would ask that the schedule be adjusted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. I don't know, Mr. Jordash, whether you had anything to do over the weekend, but -- yes. I certainly know that the interpreters have something to do over the weekend and we are already past 7.00. Could you consider when you could respond. If the Prosecution is quicker, that enables you to look at their argument first, that might speed up. At the same time, of course, the time limits were also chosen in order to give you adequate time to think about it. Could we hear from you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And the only thing I would add is that we are intending to put -- to try to file a 92 ter for the third witness so that Your Honours understand the -- the problem is not quite as imminent as it might at first appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll further hear from you tomorrow. We -- I apologise to the interpreters, technicians, and all others who are assisting us. I always forget security. We stand adjourned. We'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 24th of June, but we'll start at 1.00 p.m. So not the usual time of quarter past 2.00 but 1.00 p.m. in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of June, 2011, at 1.00 p.m. 23 24 25

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.10 p.m.,
